1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

content.thinking:
Since the camera API isn't documented and the package isn't installed to verify, I'm weighing workarounds that avoid touching `app.camera` directly—like transforming a wrapper group to fake camera movement, resetting the scene each frame, or using an orbit interaction targeting a specific node.

I think a cleaner approach is a virtual camera: nest all world content inside a mutable root group, apply the inverse of the camera transform to that group, and keep the real camera fixed at the origin looking down -Z. Lights move naturally as children of the group, but the starfield needs separate handling—rotation-only in a skybox group so stars stay distant without shifting position, though the Euler rotation order and inverse composition still need to be worked out.

To avoid Euler ambiguity, I'd use nested single-axis rotation groups—one for pitch, one for yaw, plus a translation group—so each transform is unambiguous, and I'd handle picking and focus-distance math myself since I'm not using the built-in camera pose.

Rather than guessing at an unverified `setPose` signature, I should stick to documented APIs: runtime groups with `setPosition`/`setRotation`, as shown in the robot example. That keeps things type-correct even though I'll need to flag the missing package to the user.

For the real camera, I'm setting up a perspective camera at the origin looking down -Z, with a 640x360 aspect ratio, assuming vertical FOV in the three.js style, which matters for my manual ray-picking math using tan(fov/2).

I'm making picking tolerant by using a generous hit-test radius (~14px) and choosing the nearest candidate along the ray, accepting that a horizontal-vs-vertical FOV mismatch would just shift offsets slightly. I also need to convert pointer events using the canvas bounding rect rather than relying on built-in orbit interactions, since I'm handling drag manually.

For lighting and scale, I'm planning a point light at the star with default-ish intensity/falloff, and laying out compact units: star radius 3, planet orbits roughly 8 to 40, with the overview camera positioned around 70 units away.

Now I'm working through light calibration uncertainty -- since the system isn't guaranteed to be three.js-calibrated, I'm adding ambient/hemisphere light as a baseline so objects stay visible regardless, then layering a point light at the star for directional shading, estimating intensity/decay/distance values to balance brightness against overexposure with tone mapping.

For the star's visual appearance, I'm giving it emissive glow material plus a larger transparent halo sphere using similar emissive/opacity material properties for a soft bloom-like effect.

For planet textures, I'm considering a simple procedural look through color and gradients rather than detailed surface maps, since the scope calls for basic visual variety.

Adding PBR material with white base color and high roughness so lighting reveals the spin, building a 48x32 segment sphere with unit radius scaled per planet.

Simpler to bake the radius directly into vertex positions rather than scaling nodes afterward, and I'm adding RGBA vertex colors as a Float32Array, matching the terrain example's approach which the PBR material should pick up automatically. I need to make sure winding order is outward-facing CCW for the sphere, using standard UV sphere parameterization with latitude/longitude angles to compute positions scaled by radius.

I'm working out the triangle winding by checking cross products at the equator -- testing (a, b, a+1) gave an inward-pointing normal, so I switched to (a, a+1, b) and (a+1, b+1, b) which correctly point outward.

For the rings, I'm considering building a custom flat annulus with vertex colors, double-sided by duplicating faces with reversed winding rather than relying on a flattened torus.

For orbit paths, I'm weighing whether to use a line topology geometry versus falling back on thin torus primitives, since I'm unsure if the line material setup will render correctly.

Instead I'll build a flat annulus from triangles for the orbit rings, sizing the width to stay visible despite perspective shrinkage at the overview camera distance—around 0.25 units should give roughly a pixel or so of thickness without looking too thin.

For the material, I'll use emissive color properties so the rings stay visibly lit even at grazing light angles from the center.

For the starfield, I'm placing hundreds of tiny instanced spheres at a large radius with varied colors and scale, nested inside a rotation-only sky group so the stars stay fixed relative to camera orientation but separate from the translating world group.
